triples.rationale: Nebuchadnezzar makes the image that the ensuing proclamation requires people to worship. Exodus forbids making an idol for oneself and bowing to or serving it, supplying the command opposed by this royal demand.
triples.source_text: In the eighteenth year, King Nebuchadnezzar, who administered cities and countries and all who inhabited the earth from India to Ethiopia, made a golden image, sixty cubits high and six cubits wide. He set it up on the plain of the enclosure in the country of Babylonia.

target_units.text: You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness of things in heaven above, or in the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth.

You shall not bow down to them, neither shall you serve them; for I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, repaying the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate Me,

triples.rationale: Royal officials are summoned to the image's dedication; officials later gather to inspect the men whom the fire has not harmed. The two assemblies frame demanded worship and public evidence of rescue.
triples.source_text: Nebuchadnezzar, king of kings and lord of the whole inhabited world, sent to gather all the nations, tribes, and languages, satraps, generals, district governors, consuls, administrators, those holding authority in each country, and everyone throughout the inhabited world, to come to the dedication of the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

target_units.text: The consuls, district governors, ancestral chiefs, and the king’s friends gathered. They observed those men: the fire had not touched their bodies, their hair had not burned, their trousers were unchanged, and there was no smell of fire on them.

triples.rationale: The herald addresses nations, peoples and languages before the command to worship the image. The final decree again addresses nations, tribes and languages, but now forbids blasphemy against the God who rescued the three men.
triples.source_text: The herald proclaimed to the crowds, “You are commanded, nations and countries, peoples and languages:

target_units.text: Now I decree: from every nation, every tribe, and every language, whoever blasphemes the Lord, the God of Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago, will be dismembered and his house confiscated, because there is no other god who can rescue like this.”

triples.rationale: The royal command requires bowing to a manufactured golden image. Exodus explicitly forbids bowing to or serving such images, making the conflict one of worship rather than merely disobedience to a ruler.
triples.source_text: when you hear the sound of trumpet, panpipe, kithara, sambuca, psaltery, symphonia, and every kind of musical instrument, fall down and bow to the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up.

target_units.text: You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness of things in heaven above, or in the earth beneath, or in the waters under the earth.

You shall not bow down to them, neither shall you serve them; for I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, repaying the sins of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate Me,

triples.rationale: The furnace is announced as the penalty for refusing to bow; the king later orders the three men bound and cast into it, carrying out that specific threat.
triples.source_text: They will throw into the blazing furnace anyone who does not fall down and bow.”

target_units.text: He ordered the strongest men in his force to bind Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago hand and foot and throw them into the blazing furnace.
Then those men were bound hand and foot, wearing their footwear and the tiaras on their heads, together with their clothing, and were thrown into the furnace.

Because the king’s command was urgent and the furnace had been heated seven times beyond its earlier heat, the appointed men bound them hand and foot, brought them to the furnace, and threw them into it.

triples.rationale: The nations bow when the music sounds, while the accusation singles out three Jewish officials who refuse to serve the idol or bow to the image. Their refusal contrasts with the reported public compliance.
triples.source_text: At that time, when all the nations heard the sound of the trumpet and every musical sound, all the nations, tribes, and languages fell down and bowed to the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up before him.

target_units.text: There are certain Jewish men whom you appointed over the country of Babylonia—Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago. Those men have not feared your command; they have not served your idol or bowed to your golden image that you set up.”

triples.rationale: The Chaldean accusation initiates the attack on Jewish officials over their refusal to worship the image. In the later court narrative, officials devise a religious restriction to bring Daniel down because of his prayer to God.
triples.source_text: At that time Chaldean men came forward and accused the Jews.

target_units.text: When the king decided to appoint Daniel over his whole kingdom, the two young men devised a plan and resolution together. Since they could find no sin or ignorant fault in Daniel of which they could accuse him before the king,

they said, “Come, let us establish a restriction binding upon ourselves: no one is to make a request or offer a prayer to any god for thirty days, except to King Darius; otherwise he will die.” They intended to bring Daniel down before the king and have him thrown into the lions’ pit, for they knew that Daniel prayed and entreated the Lord his God three times a day.

triples.rationale: The accusers repeat the king's command to bow to the golden image at the musical signal. The earlier proclamation supplies the specific order they invoke.
triples.source_text: You, O king, commanded and decreed that everyone who hears the trumpet and every musical sound must fall down and bow to the golden image.

target_units.text: when you hear the sound of trumpet, panpipe, kithara, sambuca, psaltery, symphonia, and every kind of musical instrument, fall down and bow to the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up.

triples.rationale: The accusers repeat the furnace penalty for refusing to bow, recalling the exact sanction already announced by the herald.
triples.source_text: Whoever does not fall down and bow will be thrown into the blazing furnace.

target_units.text: They will throw into the blazing furnace anyone who does not fall down and bow.”

triples.rationale: The accused men are named as the Jewish officials appointed over Babylonia. The earlier account records Daniel petitioning for those same three companions to be appointed over Babylonia's affairs; the accusation identifies them as appointed officials.
triples.source_text: There are certain Jewish men whom you appointed over the country of Babylonia—Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago. Those men have not feared your command; they have not served your idol or bowed to your golden image that you set up.”

target_units.text: Daniel petitioned the king that Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago be appointed over Babylonia’s affairs. Daniel remained in the royal court.

triples.rationale: The angry king has the three named men brought before him; after their preservation he calls the same men out of the furnace as servants of the Most High God. The renewed summons marks a change in his acknowledgment of them.
triples.source_text: Then Nebuchadnezzar, angered with wrath, ordered Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago brought in. The men were brought to the king.

target_units.text: The king approached the door of the furnace blazing with fire and called them by name: “Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago, servants of the Most High God of gods, come out of the fire!” Thus the men came out from the midst of the fire.

triples.rationale: The king questions their refusal to serve his gods or bow to his image. Their answer trusts the heavenly God's rescue and expressly maintains that they will not serve the idol or bow to the image.
triples.source_text: When King Nebuchadnezzar saw them, he said to them, “Why, Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago, do you not serve my gods or bow to the golden image I set up?

target_units.text: For there is a God in the heavens, our one Lord, whom we fear, who is able to rescue us from the furnace of fire; and from your hands, O king, He will rescue us.
Then it will be plain to you that we neither serve your idol nor bow to your golden image that you set up.”

triples.rationale: The king asks what god can rescue them from his hands. His later confession says their God saved them through His angel and that no other god can rescue in this way.
triples.source_text: Now, if you are ready, as soon as you hear the trumpet and every musical sound, to fall down and bow to the golden image I set up—but if not, know that unless you bow, you will immediately be thrown into the blazing furnace. What god will rescue you from my hands?”

target_units.text: King Nebuchadnezzar spoke and said, “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago, who sent His angel and saved His servants who hoped in Him. They rejected the king’s command and surrendered their bodies to burning so that they would neither serve nor bow to another god except their own God.

Now I decree: from every nation, every tribe, and every language, whoever blasphemes the Lord, the God of Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago, will be dismembered and his house confiscated, because there is no other god who can rescue like this.”

triples.rationale: The three men declare that their God can and will rescue them from the furnace and the king. The witnesses subsequently find them unburned, and the king acknowledges that their God saved them.
triples.source_text: For there is a God in the heavens, our one Lord, whom we fear, who is able to rescue us from the furnace of fire; and from your hands, O king, He will rescue us.

target_units.text: The consuls, district governors, ancestral chiefs, and the king’s friends gathered. They observed those men: the fire had not touched their bodies, their hair had not burned, their trousers were unchanged, and there was no smell of fire on them.

triples.rationale: The men state that they neither serve the king's idol nor bow to it. Their stated allegiance corresponds to the command to have no other gods and not bow to or serve manufactured images.
triples.source_text: Then it will be plain to you that we neither serve your idol nor bow to your golden image that you set up.”

triples.rationale: The king orders the furnace heated sevenfold. The later description of its fueling explicitly reports the sevenfold heating, connecting the command with its execution.
triples.source_text: Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the appearance of his face changed. He ordered the furnace heated seven times beyond what it needed to be heated.

target_units.text: The king’s servants who threw them in did not stop heating the furnace. When they threw the three together into the furnace, the furnace was sevenfold ablaze in its heat. When they threw them in, those casting them were above them, while others stoked beneath them with naphtha, tow, pitch, and vine brushwood.

triples.rationale: The king orders the men bound hand and foot and thrown into the furnace; he later sees them walking unbound in the fire without harm. The reversal concerns the stated bonds as well as survival.
triples.source_text: He ordered the strongest men in his force to bind Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago hand and foot and throw them into the blazing furnace.

target_units.text: “Behold! I see four men unbound, walking in the fire, and no harm has come upon them. The fourth has the likeness of an angel of God.”

triples.rationale: The men are thrown into the furnace still clothed. The later inspection finds unchanged trousers, unburned hair and no smell of fire, making their bodily and material preservation explicit.
triples.source_text: Then those men were bound hand and foot, wearing their footwear and the tiaras on their heads, together with their clothing, and were thrown into the furnace.

target_units.text: The consuls, district governors, ancestral chiefs, and the king’s friends gathered. They observed those men: the fire had not touched their bodies, their hair had not burned, their trousers were unchanged, and there was no smell of fire on them.

triples.rationale: The narrative repeats the sevenfold heating and the binding and casting of the men, showing that the king's preceding orders have been carried out.
triples.source_text: Because the king’s command was urgent and the furnace had been heated seven times beyond its earlier heat, the appointed men bound them hand and foot, brought them to the furnace, and threw them into it.

He ordered the strongest men in his force to bind Sedrach, Misach, and Abdenago hand and foot and throw them into the blazing furnace.

triples.rationale: The flame kills those who bound the companions while preserving the companions themselves. The later inspection supplies public evidence of their preservation: untouched bodies and no fire damage.
triples.source_text: The flame came out of the furnace and burned and killed the men who had bound Azariah and his companions; but they themselves were preserved.

target_units.text: The consuls, district governors, ancestral chiefs, and the king’s friends gathered. They observed those men: the fire had not touched their bodies, their hair had not burned, their trousers were unchanged, and there was no smell of fire on them.

triples.rationale: The worshippers are named Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael, the Judean names of the three companions introduced with Daniel. This links the prayer to the youths known elsewhere in the episode by court names.
triples.source_text: Thus Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael prayed and sang to the Lord when the king ordered them thrown into the furnace.

target_units.text: Among the lineage of Israel’s sons from Judea were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

triples.rationale: Azariah and his companions pray and give thanks amid the fire while their captors stoke it. Paul and Silas likewise pray and sing hymns while confined with their feet secured in stocks.
triples.source_text: Azariah stood and prayed in this manner. Opening his mouth, he gave thanks to the Lord together with his companions amid the fire, while the Chaldeans were fiercely stoking the furnace. They said:

target_units.text: Having received such an order, he put them in the inner prison and secured their feet in the stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, while the prisoners listened to them.

triples.rationale: Azariah's prayer blesses the God of the fathers and His enduring name. The later communal hymn opens with that same blessing of the fathers' God and His name.
triples.source_text: “Blessed art Thou, Lord, God of our fathers; Thy name is praised and glorified for ever.

target_units.text: “Blessed art Thou, Lord, God of our fathers, praised and highly exalted for ever. Blessed is the holy name of Thy glory, exceedingly praised and highly exalted through all ages.

triples.rationale: Azariah confesses that God's deeds and judgments are righteous. Daniel's later prayer likewise calls God righteous in the calamities brought upon a people who did not obey His voice.
triples.source_text: For Thou art righteous in everything Thou hast done to us; all Thy works are true, Thy ways upright, and all Thy judgments true.

target_units.text: The Lord God kept watch over the calamities and brought them upon us, for the Lord our God is righteous in everything He may do, and we did not listen to His voice.

triples.rationale: The prayer attributes Jerusalem's judgment to the people's sins. Daniel later appeals for wrath to turn from Jerusalem while confessing that the people's sins made the city and people a reproach.
triples.source_text: Thou hast carried out judgments of truth in everything Thou didst bring upon us and upon Thy holy city, our fathers’ Jerusalem. For in truth and judgment Thou didst all these things because of our sins.

target_units.text: Master, according to Thy righteousness, let Thy wrath and anger turn away from Thy city Jerusalem, Thy holy mountain. Because of our sins and our fathers’ acts of ignorance, Jerusalem and Thy people, Lord, are a reproach among all around us.

triples.rationale: Both prayers confess collective sin, lawless conduct and departure from God's commands, placing the speakers within the people's wrongdoing rather than treating them as detached observers.
triples.source_text: For we have sinned in everything and acted lawlessly by departing from Thee. We have sinned in everything and have not obeyed the commands of Thy law.

target_units.text: we have sinned, done wrong, acted impiously, fallen away, and transgressed Thy commandments and judgments,

triples.rationale: Azariah says the people failed to keep the commands given for their good; Daniel's later confession says Israel refused God's voice and abandoned the law, bringing its curse upon them.
triples.source_text: We have neither kept nor done what Thou didst command us, so that it might go well with us.

target_units.text: and have not listened to the voice of the Lord our God, to follow Thy law that Thou didst set before Moses and us through Thy servants the prophets.
All Israel abandoned Thy law and fell away, refusing to hear Thy voice. The curse and oath written in the law of Moses, God’s servant, came upon us, because we sinned against Him.

triples.rationale: The prayer calls the judgments brought upon the people true. Daniel's later prayer similarly says the announced calamities came according to the covenant and affirms God's righteousness in them.
triples.source_text: And now, everything Thou hast brought upon us and everything Thou hast done to us, Thou hast done in true judgment.

target_units.text: He established for us His commands, all He spoke against us and against our judges, all Thou didst judge for us, bringing great calamities upon us, such as had not occurred under heaven as occurred in Jerusalem.

According to what is written in Moses’ covenant, all the calamities came upon us. Yet we did not seek the face of the Lord our God by departing from our sins and understanding Thy righteousness, Lord.
The Lord God kept watch over the calamities and brought them upon us, for the Lord our God is righteous in everything He may do, and we did not listen to His voice.

triples.rationale: Azariah describes being handed over to hostile enemies and an unjust king. Chronicles likewise describes God handing the people into Chaldean power, followed by destruction and captivity; the shared connection is the judgment of exile.
triples.source_text: Thou didst hand us over to our enemies, lawless and most hateful apostates, and to an unjust king, the most wicked in all the earth.

target_units.text: He brought against them a king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword in the house of his sanctuary and did not spare Zedekiah. They had no mercy on their virgins and carried away their elders. He handed everything into their hands.
All the vessels of God’s house, great and small, the treasures, and all the treasures of the king and the magnates—he brought everything into Babylon.
He burned the Lord’s house, demolished Jerusalem’s wall, and burned its citadels with fire, consigning every beautiful article to destruction.
He deported the survivors to Babylon, and they became slaves to him and his sons until the kingdom of the Medes,

triples.rationale: The speakers confess shame and inability to answer before God. Daniel's later prayer similarly contrasts God's righteousness with the shame of Judah, Jerusalem, Israel and their rulers because of sin.
triples.source_text: Now we cannot open our mouths; shame and reproach have come upon Thy servants and those who revere Thee.

target_units.text: Righteousness belongs to Thee, Lord, but shame of face to us as on this day—to the people of Judah, those dwelling in Jerusalem, and all the people Israel, near and far, in all the countries where Thou didst scatter them because of the trespass they committed before Thee.
Master, shame of face belongs to us, to our kings, rulers, and fathers, because we have sinned against Thee.

triples.rationale: The prayer asks God not to abandon or destroy His people or dissolve the covenant. In Leviticus God says He did not disregard them in enemy territory so as to consume them or dissolve His covenant, and that He will remember it. The petition appeals to that covenant fidelity.
triples.source_text: Do not hand us over utterly, for Thy name’s sake; do not dissolve Thy covenant.

target_units.text: And yet even so, while they were in their enemies’ land, I did not disregard them or become indignant with them so as to consume them and dissolve My covenant with them, for I am the Lord their God.
And I will remember for them the former covenant, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of a house of slavery, before the nations to be their God. I am the Lord.
